vignette:
He is 38, married, and has spent most of his adult life in classrooms, speaking with the steady patience of a teacher who is used to holding other people's attention. Before the assault, he thinks of himself as careful but not fearful. He walks the same route home from school most afternoons, usually with papers under one arm and lesson plans folded in his bag, stopping sometimes to answer a student's question or to buy milk on the way. He and his wife have a routine that feels solid and familiar, the kind built from ordinary repetitions.

That changes one evening when he is mugged on a quiet street a few blocks from home. It happens fast enough that later he has trouble placing the exact sequence in order. A man steps close, too close, then another. He notices the smell of alcohol, the shine of one face under a streetlamp, the sudden hard pressure of a hand against his chest. When the demand comes, his body reacts before his mind does. He gives up his wallet, then his phone, then his watch, hands shaking so badly he can barely unclasp the strap. One of the men grabs him by the collar and shoves him against a wall. His head snaps back. He remembers the scrape of brick against his shoulder and the strange, humiliating thought that he is being treated like an object, not a person. The men leave him standing there, breathing too fast, with his heart pounding so hard he can hear it in his ears.

In the days after, he tells himself he is mostly fine. He goes to work because he does not know what else to do. In class, he stands in front of his students and feels a thin layer of unreality between himself and the room, as if he is speaking from farther away than usual. He catches himself scanning the windows and the hallway whenever someone moves in the corridor. Loud voices make him jump. The first time a student slams a desk, he flinches so sharply that the class goes quiet, and he feels heat rise in his face. He laughs it off, but afterward he sits at his desk longer than necessary, staring at the wall and trying to slow his breathing.

At home, he becomes increasingly preoccupied with doors, locks, and where everyone is standing. He checks the front lock twice, then again before bed. His wife notices he is tense in the evenings, saying little, and that he startles if she approaches him from behind. He tries to explain that he is just tired, that it was only a robbery, not "that bad," but the words do not settle him. He begins avoiding the route where it happened and invents reasons to drive rather than walk, even for short distances. He does not like the feeling of being outside after dark. When he does have to leave school late for parent meetings or grading, he finds himself looking over his shoulder every few minutes, convincing himself that any group of men nearby is a threat.

Sleep becomes difficult. He falls asleep exhausted and wakes an hour later with his chest tight and his mind already racing. Sometimes he dreams of being pinned against the wall, though the details shift: the men's faces are blurred, the street keeps changing, and in the dream he is always trying to speak but no sound comes out. He wakes sweaty and disoriented, then lies still so he will not disturb his wife. Some nights he gets up and sits in the dark kitchen, listening to the house, feeling ashamed of how long it takes his body to settle.

He also notices that certain moments pull him back into the assault without warning. The metallic rattle of a gate, footsteps coming up behind him, even a student's hand grabbing his sleeve can make his stomach drop and his muscles tense before he can think. He hates that his mind does this. As a teacher, he is used to being composed, to having language for other people's feelings, yet with this experience he cannot find words that feel large enough. He grows quieter with colleagues and more irritable with his wife, then feels guilty and withdraws further.

Over time, his world narrows. He still teaches, still grades papers at the dining room table, still attends to the practical details of marriage and work, but he does so with effort that now seems to cost him more than it used to. He moves through daily life alert for danger, carrying the assault in his body as much as in his memory, never fully at ease when he is outside, and not entirely at ease when he is home either.
